issues.legal_issue: Unreliable test identification evidence does not prevent a finding of identity when credible in-court identification is supported by reliable circumstantial evidence.
material_facts: Three witnesses testified that they saw the assault and identified the accused in court; their presence near the scene was natural, and they had no apparent animus against him.

The court considered the identification parades of little value, but the witnesses’ in-court identifications were supported by evidence that the accused had purchased the iron pipe used in the assault, led police to its recovery, and had human blood on his clothes when arrested.
Medical evidence showed that the victim’s injuries could have been caused by the recovered pipe and were sufficient to cause death.
issues.conclusion: The identification parades were of little value, but the credible in-court identifications, corroborating circumstances, and medical evidence reliably established the accused’s identity and guilt.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 9 of the Evidence Act, test identification evidence is admissible but is only supporting evidence: it may corroborate a witness’s substantive in-court identification, and has no independent value by itself. Test identification is not the only means of confirmation; circumstantial evidence may also establish identity. The court cited no earlier case for this principle.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and credible_in_court_identification and reliable_circumstantial_corroboration and medical_evidence_supports_the_account

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: A person challenged a criminal conviction in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.credible_in_court_identification: Witnesses who were naturally present at the scene identified the accused in court, and the court found their testimony trustworthy.
predicates.reliable_circumstantial_corroboration: Independent circumstances linked the accused to the weapon or its recovery and to physical evidence connected with the assault.
predicates.medical_evidence_supports_the_account: Medical evidence was consistent with the described weapon and injuries and supported the cause of death.
predicates.conviction_supported_by_reliable_evidenc: The conviction rests on reliable evidence establishing the accused’s guilt.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal from conviction includes credible in-court identification, reliable circumstantial corroboration, and supporting medical evidence, the conviction is supported by reliable evidence.

issues.legal_issue: Discrepancies about details of an assault do not by themselves discredit eyewitness testimony when the witnesses agree on the essential account.
material_facts: The witnesses differed about the precise number of blows and whether the victim was standing or lying during the assault.
The court found that the differences concerned details and that the witnesses agreed on the essential account; their presence at the scene was natural and probable.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancies were natural variations in observation, perception, and memory and were not a ground for rejecting the eyewitness evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Differences in witnesses’ faculties of observation, perception, and memory naturally produce variations in details. Such discrepancies do not justify rejecting testimony when there is agreement on the substratum of the case. The court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: A person challenged a criminal conviction in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.discrepancies_confined_to_details: Witnesses differed about incidental particulars rather than the central events they described.
predicates.witnesses_agree_on_essential_account: Witnesses gave a substantially consistent account of the essential events.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal from conviction involves discrepancies confined to details and witnesses agree on the essential account, minor variations do not discredit the witnesses.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must give reasons when summarily disposing of an appeal that raises arguable questions of fact or law.
material_facts: The High Court summarily dismissed the criminal appeal without recording reasons.
The appeal raised questions of fact and law concerning guilt or innocence.
The Supreme Court declined to remit the matter because doing so would cause further delay and instead examined the evidence itself.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have dismissed the appeal without a reasoned order; however, the Supreme Court did not remit the case and independently considered the evidence to avoid further delay.
issues.legal_principle: An appeal raising arguable factual or legal questions should not be summarily dismissed without a reasoned order. The court relied on Article 136 of the Constitution and Shri Mohamad Ali v. State of Maharashtra.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: A person challenged a criminal conviction in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.appeal_raised_arguable_questions: The appeal presented factual or legal questions reasonably calling for appellate consideration.
predicates.appellate_court_disposed_without_reasons: The appellate court dismissed the appeal without recording reasons.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal from conviction raises arguable questions and the appellate court disposes of it without reasons, the appellate court must give a reasoned decision.
